summary.title: Advice for new software devs who've read all those other advice essays
summary.one_liner: Thirteen contrarian, sometimes contradictory tips for early-career programmers on evaluating advice, avoiding the "Right Way" trap, and understanding why software trends come and go.
takeaways: Evaluate advice on its merits rather than the speaker's reputation, since writing skill often drives influence more than expertise.
Look for the 'horror story' or historical origin behind a best practice to decide whether it applies to you.
Try several kinds of programming early on (frontend, backend, ops, databases) to find work you enjoy.
Be conservative with new technologies: software hype spreads fast, so many tools with small userbases never get wide adoption.
summary.summary: The author, Hillel Wayne, responds to a request for advice for early-career programmers by offering thirteen short, personal tips, some intentionally contradictory. Topics include not over-trusting any single authority, reading the book Debugging: The 9 Rules, resisting becoming a "Right Way Guy" about any methodology, and treating best practices as path-dependent things with historical "horror stories" behind them. Other tips cover taking walks, learning the hidden depth of common tools, talking to non-engineering staff, trying different kinds of programming, and why software technology hype spreads quickly and warrants caution. It is an opinion essay with no code or tutorial steps.
